Many of you came here after seeing a moderator commit abusive behavior in a particular sub. You were promised that the mods of this brand new sub were much more open about posts and less inclined to censor anyone. But promises are just words; meaningless unless you take action to fullfill those promises. So here is the action.

We are introducing new rules. These are not rules for you to follow regarding what to post. We are posting rules for us, the moderators, on how we think we should be held accountable. We write these rules confident that we will not abuse them now, we write them as a contingency plan for the longterm. These rules will hold all current, and future, moderators in check and prevent them from committing abusive behavior. Here they are:

  1. Moderators are not leaders; we are here to only clean up the shit, not drive the discussion in a way we favor it. Moderators can only remove posts that either violate Voat's rules, create spam, or does not create absolutely any discussion at all. The discussion topics of this community is utterly up to the users.

  2. A three strike system for all banning. If we must ban a user, two of the mods must be in agreement. The initial ban will only be for 24 hours. If the user strikes again, 72. Again, and it would be a permanent ban.

  3. The community can voice their dissent if they see a mod acting in a way they do not like. In order to call a mod into question, they must submit a post containing legitimate proof that the mod is committing abusive behavior. If that post is agreed by the community(95% agreement with 100 upvotes minimum(this may be subject to scaling as we grow)), a vote of no confidence will be held. The vote will happen over a 24 hour period and require a two thirds majority for a mod to be cast out. The subverse will go private in that circumstance to ensure that no vote brigading occurs. In order to prevent popularity contests, the moderators reserve the right to pick the new mods. The new mods will be subject to these rules.

We understand many of you might not care about this. But since /v/askgoat is a discussion oriented sub, we felt it was necessary to ensure a backup plan should any of our mods commit abuse. We also understand rule 3 might still pose problems, but we can discuss a better system for mod accountability. To ensure that there have been no "backroom deals" between mods, heres a link to the public subverse /v/askgoatmodtalk, which was where the discussion about moderator rules took place. We hope these rules will make you look at us favorably and also hope that these rules remain a constant reminder of all moderators of the responsibility they have with running /v/askgoat. Please post your thoughts and questions below. We would love to hear them.

I subscribed to /v/AskGoat, and I'm excited to see where the sub goes, but I wanted to comment and say that I'm not a fan of giving moderators restrictions, and this is why:

When you give moderators restrictions, the assumption is that they can do anything outside of those restrictions. I'd rather see a system where moderators are given powers, and the assumption is that they can't do anything outside of those powers. Rule 1 is already written like a power:

Moderators can only remove posts that either violate Voat's rules, create spam, or does not create absolutely any discussion at all.

It grants mods the power to remove posts that fit [criteria X] with the assumption that mods cannot remove posts outside of that power.

Rule 2 is a little more like a restriction:

If we must ban a user, two of the mods must be in agreement.

This is a restriction because it restricts a mod's ability to ban without really addressing what mods can ban people for. This rule would be better written as a power:

mods can ban users who [criteria X], as long as [two mods are in agreement]

The assumption here is that mods have no ban power outside of [criteria X] and only when two mods are in agreement.

Most modern governments are set up with this in mind: citizens have rights, and the government has powers. The government has no power outside what is written in law, and citizens have total rights outside of what is written in law. If there is no law for a given situation, the assumption is that It's a good system, and it's pretty close to what most subs already use (a list of posting rules that mods can legitimately remove posts for). I think that implementing a system of restrictions on mods is a step back and can fall apart as soon as you have rogue mods in power. A better system would be to have a list of granted powers, with the assumption being that mods have no power outside the ones listed.

To add context, I brought up this opinion in another thread and /u/TheKillerRabbit offered a good rebuttal. I'm linking that conversation here for anyone who wants to read the discussion from both sides.
